name: Benko Gambit
summary: The Benko Gambit (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5) sacrifices a wing pawn for lasting pressure on the open a- and b-files.
intro: The Benko Gambit, also called the Volga Gambit, arises after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5. Black offers a wing pawn to prise open the a- and b-files, aiming the fianchettoed g7-bishop and heavy pieces at White's queenside for pressure that can persist deep into the endgame.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining idea is the pawn sacrifice 3...b5, offering material to open the a- and b-files. After 4.cxb5 a6 Black recaptures, fianchettoes with ...g6 and ...Bg7, castles, and plays ...d6, then piles rooks on the half-open queenside files while the queen often settles on a5. What makes the gambit unusual is that the compensation is positional and long-lasting rather than a quick attack: Black's pressure against White's queenside frequently endures even after the queens are exchanged.

White, for his part, is a clean pawn up and tries to convert that material once Black's activity is contained. The struggle revolves around the entrenched d5-pawn, which grants White space, and the two half-open files that give Black his play. If White can complete development, neutralise the long dark-squared diagonal, and trade off Black's active pieces, the extra pawn should tell; if not, the queenside pressure can become a permanent nuisance.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: In the Fully Accepted lines White plays 5.bxa6, when Black recaptures with 5...Bxa6 (or first inserts 5...g6), obtaining the two open files and rapid piece activity in return for the pawn. A key modern try is the King Walk, where after ...Bxf1 White answers Kxf1 and then unravels with g3 and Kg2, sidestepping the loss of castling rights while keeping the extra pawn.

White can also decline. The Half-Accepted 5.b6 returns the pawn immediately to keep the queenside files closed and blunt Black's pressure, while quieter setups with 5.e3 or an early Nc3 and Nf3 aim to hold the extra pawn behind a solid structure. Independent tries such as 4.Nf3 and 4.Nd2 avoid the main structures altogether, steering the game into calmer channels.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The gambit's Volga name traces to Russian analysis around the middle of the twentieth century, a reference to the Volga river. It was popularised in the West by the Hungarian-American grandmaster Pal Benko, who developed its ideas and wrote an influential monograph, and the opening has carried his name in English ever since. Prized for offering Black clear, durable compensation rather than a speculative attack, it became a respected weapon at every level and remains a practical way to unbalance the game against 1.d4.

keyIdeas: The pawn sacrifice ...b5 opens the a- and b-files for queenside pressure.
Compensation is positional and long-lasting, not a quick attack.
The fianchettoed g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal at White's queenside.
Black doubles rooks on the half-open files and posts the queen on a5.
Black's pressure often persists even after queens are exchanged.
White's trumps are the extra pawn and the space-gaining d5-pawn.

white: Complete development and consolidate the extra pawn safely.
Return the pawn at the right moment to blunt Black's file pressure.
Meet ...Bxf1 with Kxf1 and unravel via g3 and Kg2 (the King Walk).
Contest the a- and b-files and trade off Black's active pieces.
Use the d5-pawn's space to restrain Black and seek central play.
black: Play ...a6 and recapture to open the a- and b-files.
Fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7 to pressure the long diagonal.
Double rooks on the half-open files and post the queen on a5.
Manoeuvre ...Nbd7 and ...Ra7-b7 to intensify queenside pressure.
Keep pressing into the endgame, where the compensation endures.
